Then, I will consider the implications of rapid technological change for the economy more broadly, including for aggregate supply and demand, for inflation, and for the labor market. Finally, I will discuss briefly my thinking about the economic outlook and monetary policy. Productivity Puzzles: Then and Now Nobel Prize-winning economist [OFFICIAL] Solow famously wrote in 1987 that "you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics."3 He may have been expecting too much from the computers he saw. While 32 percent of workers used computers at work in 1989, the computers were not very powerful. To illustrate, the processor in your phone today can do about as many calculations per second as 10 million 1987 vintage personal computers (PCs).4 In the aggregate, national spending on computers—shown in figure 1—was barely detectable at the time, despite PCs being an important part of the zeitgeist.5 Ten years later, computer investment had taken off and some observers, notably [OFFICIAL], believed they could see it in the productivity statistics, though the link between the two was only established later.6 Investment in information technology (IT) capital—computers, software, and communications equipment—increased the annual growth rate of labor productivity about 3/4 percentage point in the late 1990s.7 While that expansion of the IT capital stock directly boosted worker productivity, there was more than that to the IT boom.

Implications for the Macroeconomy What does all this mean for my thinking about macroeconomic activity? My baseline view is that adoption of new technology will ultimately lift the economy's productive capacity substantially but gradually. Expectations of those longer-term gains on the supply side of the economy are already increasing aggregate demand significantly. A substantial portion of the rise in equity prices over the past few years can be attributed to enthusiasm around the new technology. That added wealth appears to be raising household spending. Firms are building and equipping new data centers on a very large scale to support model training and inference, driving rapid growth in aggregate business investment.18 This spending is putting upward pressure on resource utilization and the general price level.

In addition, because investment demand is concentrated in some sectors where supply has struggled to keep pace, such as memory and logic chips, it has also contributed to steep increases in prices of specific goods. Over the medium term, the supply of these goods should catch up, and the broader boost to aggregate productivity from adoption should materialize.19 Both of those developments should ease the upward pressure on prices we see today. While the new technology should ultimately generate higher output and income in the aggregate, I recognize that this transition could be painful for some workers and businesses. Firms that lag in adoption could be at a competitive disadvantage, and their long-term viability could be at risk. And even at firms that successfully adopt the technology, workers who specialize in tasks that AI can perform more efficiently—such as certain aspects of software development—may face job displacement.

One risk to my baseline outlook is that the new technology could displace workers much faster than they can adapt and retrain, which could result in an increase in unemployment. In this scenario, a key question for monetary policy would be how much of this increase is structural—reflecting a persistent mismatch between worker skills and firms' needs—and therefore likely to persist even when the economy is operating close to its full potential. Monetary policy can affect cyclical conditions, like a temporary downturn in employment and spending, but it cannot address the structural factors that determine long-run rates of employment. As a monetary policymaker, I must also consider the potential effects of the new technology on the longer-run neutral rate of interest, often called r*.

If the neutral rate rises, then for any given level of the federal funds rate, policy effectively becomes more accommodative. Conversely, if the neutral rate declines, then policy effectively becomes more restrictive. If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms' desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates. As I discussed earlier, higher productivity growth may also discourage household savings and raise consumption by increasing expected future income. Under these circumstances, to reconcile the increase in investment with reduced savings, the neutral rate would likely rise. However, predicting changes in the neutral rate of interest is challenging, given the historically noisy relationship between productivity growth and real interest rates.

Policymakers must remain attentive to real-time developments and potential future developments to ensure that the stance of monetary policy remains appropriately calibrated. [OFFICIAL] Outlook While the rapid pace of technological change has understandably captured the public's attention, as a monetary policymaker my charge is to consider the broader economy, and not just a single sector. Therefore, I will use the last portion of my talk to discuss my current economic outlook for the U.S. and the stance of monetary policy. The economy has gained momentum this year, expanding at a pace roughly in line with its potential. That consistent growth is notable because the economy has faced a cascade of shocks, including an energy shock, and significant changes in trade policy, in addition to the technology buildout.

As you can see in figure 4, GDP expanded at a 3.4 percent pace in the third quarter. Business investment has been quite strong. Consumer spending has remained resilient. I expect the expansion will continue roughly in line with potential output next year. A broad range of recent data from the labor market shows conditions have stabilized. Figure 5 shows that the unemployment rate has largely moved sideways this year, settling at 4.1 percent in October. Layoffs remain low, and job openings have moved a bit higher. While job creation has been volatile, payroll gains have broadened to many sectors in recent months, which I find encouraging. I expect the unemployment rate to stay around its current level in the near term—a level I view as consistent with maximum employment.

The risks to my economic output and employment forecasts are roughly balanced. An increase in uncertainty tied to Middle East tensions may weigh on activity and hiring, while a further surge in investment spending could support stronger growth. Turning to the price-stability side of our dual mandate, inflation remains notably above the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) 2 percent target. The 12-month change in the personal consumption expenditures price index, the blue line in figure 6, was 3.6 percent in September. Higher energy costs are one of the drivers of elevated inflation. Oil prices have been quite volatile, and global energy supplies have come under renewed strain, reflecting heightened geopolitical tensions. I remain concerned about the risk of higher energy prices leading to a persistent rise in inflation more broadly.

The 12-month change in core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices and is shown by the dashed red dashed line, was 3.1 percent in September. Indirectly, higher energy costs are showing through in certain areas including airfares and transportation, and the boom in demand for new technologies has been driving unusually strong cost increases for consumer goods and services that depend on the same inputs, like memory. Data received so far for October remains consistent with well above-target inflation. I am also paying close attention to inflation expectations. Survey-based, short-term measures of inflation expectations are elevated, mainly reflecting higher energy prices. Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations, however, have remained stable at levels consistent with 2 percent inflation.

At the FOMC policy meeting last month, I joined the majority of my colleagues in voting to hold the federal funds rate steady, as shown in figure 7. Data received since that meeting have been consistent with economic activity and labor market conditions remaining broadly solid, while inflation readings show persistent price pressures. Accordingly, I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy. Going forward, I believe that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks. Conclusion In conclusion, I will leave you with this thought: [OFFICIAL] technologies cause us to revisit old but very important questions.

The paths from innovation to adoption and adaptation to durable productivity gains can be uneven and unpredictable. Some would even say, puzzling. [OFFICIAL] technologies command our attention long before they affect measured productivity. They cause us to rethink our understanding of how the economy works. Re-understanding our economy makes the process of monetary policymaking exciting and challenging. Thankfully, through it all, our mission at the Fed is clear. Deliver on the dual mandate given to us by Congress: maximum employment and price stability. These are the goals of every action we take. [OFFICIAL] you for your time today.
